title: How the world reaches India: six sources, five pipes
hook:
Imagine three headlines landing on your phone before the market opens. The US Federal Reserve has held rates but sounds grumpy about inflation. A tanker has been hit near the Gulf. And Washington has announced another round of tariffs, this time naming India. Which of these should worry you, which stocks will feel it, and when?

Most investors treat global news as weather: the Nifty goes red, you wait for it to pass. But foreign shocks do not arrive at random. They come in through a small number of pipes, and each pipe empties into a different part of the Indian market at a different speed. A Fed surprise can move the rupee before lunch; a tariff can take two quarters to reach an exporter's revenue.

This chapter is the map. Six outside economies matter for Indian markets, and they reach us through only five channels. Learn the channels and every scary headline becomes a much simpler question: which pipe is this coming through, and who is standing at the other end?
short: Six outside economies matter most for India, and they reach us through just five channels: rates and the dollar, commodity prices, trade and tariffs, capital flows, and energy supply.

The channels run at very different speeds. Money moves in days, commodity costs reach margins within a quarter, tariffs take quarters, and an energy supply shock hits prices at once and the budget for months.
A single foreign event usually travels through two or three channels at once, so one headline can hurt banks, carmakers and IT firms for different reasons.
India is now owned as a market in its own right, so its valuation premium is more sensitive to US rates and less to trouble in its neighbours.
Today three of the five channels point the wrong way at once: rates, energy supply and trade. The combination, not any single one, is what makes this shock serious.

sections.heading: Six taps, five pipes, four places it lands
sections.html:
Start with who matters. The United States sets the price of money for the whole planet and is India's biggest export market. China sets the price of most manufactured goods and of the metals and chemicals that go into them. Europe buys Indian goods and services and houses many of the funds that own Indian shares. Japan, through its ultra-low interest rates, has long been a source of cheap money sloshing around global markets. The Gulf sells us most of our oil and gas and employs millions of Indians who send money home. And Russia, since 2022, has become one of India's largest suppliers of crude.

Now the pipes. Whatever happens in those six places reaches India in one of five ways. It changes interest rates and the dollar. It changes commodity prices. It changes trade, through demand or tariffs. It changes capital flows, meaning how much foreign money wants to own Indian assets. Or it changes the physical supply of energy, which is not the same as its price.

[[fig:1]]

Read the diagram from left to right: where a shock starts, the pipe it travels through, and where India feels it. Notice two things. First, the United States has lines running into three different pipes, which is why a single Fed meeting can hit the rupee, foreign flows and exporters on the same day. Second, everything eventually pours into just four buckets on the right: the rupee and reserves, inflation, corporate margins and equity flows.

Here's the useful habit: when a foreign headline breaks, don't ask whether it is good or bad for India. Ask which pipe it is in and which bucket it fills.

sections.heading: Why speed is the first question to ask
sections.html:
The five channels do not just differ in what they hit. They differ in how fast. And speed is what decides whether a shock is a bad week or a bad year.

  • Rates and capital flows move in days. When US yields jump, foreign funds can sell Indian shares the same afternoon and the rupee weakens by the next morning. The pain is quick, loud and often partly reversed.
  • Commodity prices reach margins within a quarter. A paint company does not feel crude-based raw materials at today's price. It feels them when the inventory it bought earlier runs out and the new, dearer batch flows into its costs. So margin hits show up in the results season after the spike, not during it.
  • Trade and tariffs take quarters. Orders are placed months ahead. A garment exporter hit by a new tariff keeps shipping existing orders for a while; the damage arrives when the buyer stops placing new ones. You see it first in order books and commentary, much later in revenue.
  • Energy supply is the exception. If oil cannot physically reach you, pump prices, freight and airline fares can reprice on the same day. And then the slow damage begins: the government cuts fuel taxes or raises subsidies to cushion people, and that strain on the budget lasts for months.

Think of a bowler's repertoire. A bouncer is frightening but over in a second; a slow off-break does more damage over a long spell.

Fast channels frighten the market. Slow channels change the earnings.

sections.heading: Money moves first: rates, the dollar and foreign flows
sections.html:
The fastest pipe carries money itself. Foreign portfolio investors, the global pension, sovereign and mutual funds that buy Indian shares and bonds, own a large slice of India's biggest companies. They compare what they can earn in India with what they can earn safely at home. When US government bonds pay more, India has to work harder to justify the risk, and some of that money goes home.

The selling hits in a particular order. It starts with the most liquid large caps, the banks and blue chips that foreign funds own in size, because those are the easiest to sell quickly. Then comes the currency. To take money out, a foreign fund sells rupees and buys dollars, which pushes the rupee down. A weaker rupee makes the remaining foreign holdings worth less in dollars, which can trigger more selling. That loop is why outflows come in waves.

What has changed over the last decade is who stands on the other side. Indian households now pour money into the market every month through systematic investment plans in mutual funds, and domestic institutions buy what foreigners sell. In earlier crises, foreign selling met thin domestic demand and prices fell off a cliff. Today the same selling often meets a steady domestic bid. The rupee still feels it, but the index falls less than it used to.

So when foreign investors are heavy sellers, check how much domestic institutions bought and what the rupee did. If domestic buying absorbed it, the pipe was busy but the bucket did not overflow.

sections.heading: Commodities: the bill arrives within a quarter
sections.html:
India imports a lot of what its factories and kitchens run on: crude oil, gold, coal, edible oils, fertilisers, electronic components. So when the world price of a commodity rises, India mostly pays it. That is the commodity pipe, and it fills two buckets: inflation for households and margins for companies.

The margin story is where investors can get ahead. A rise in crude raises costs for paint makers, tyre companies, plastics and chemicals, airlines and anyone running trucks. Coal hits cement and power; palm oil squeezes soap and snack makers. Each can pass some of it on, but rarely all and rarely at once. The squeeze shows up in the quarter or two after the spike, and the relief shows up a quarter or two after prices fall. That lag is predictable, which makes it useful.

A few Indian companies are on the other side of the trade: metal producers, upstream oil explorers, coal miners. When the global price of their product rises, so do their earnings. That is why metal stocks often rise just when the rest of the market worries about inflation.

One indicator worth knowing is the price of copper against gold. Copper is the metal of factories and construction; gold is what people buy when they are scared. When copper is beating gold, the world is betting on growth. When gold is beating copper, it is betting on trouble. Crude, but it tells you whether a commodity rise comes from a booming world, which Indian cyclicals can ride, or from fear, which they cannot.

sections.heading: Trade and tariffs: the slow channel that changes business models
sections.html:
The trade pipe is the slowest and the easiest to underestimate. It runs both ways. India sells software services, pharmaceuticals, garments, gems and jewellery, seafood, auto parts and engineering goods to the world, mostly to the US and Europe. And it buys manufactured goods, mostly from China.

On the export side, demand and tariffs matter. When American companies tighten budgets, Indian IT firms see deal sizes shrink a few quarters later. When the US raises tariffs on Indian goods, clusters that sell heavily to America, such as the garment towns of Tamil Nadu, the diamond workshops of Surat or the shrimp farms of the east coast, feel it first in cancelled or delayed orders. Listed companies report it later.

On the import side, the big force is China. When Chinese factories have spare capacity, as they often do when their own economy slows, they sell steel, chemicals and solar panels abroad at prices Indian producers struggle to match. Great for Indian buyers of those goods, painful for Indian makers. It is why India so often reaches for anti-dumping duties.

And sometimes trade shocks create opportunity. When the US and China started their tariff war, global companies began looking for a second factory outside China, a strategy known as China plus one. India has been one of the beneficiaries, most visibly in phone assembly. Trade shocks are slow, but they can redraw where things get made.

sections.heading: Energy supply: when price is not the problem, quantity is
sections.html:
Why separate energy supply from commodity prices? In a normal commodity rise, oil is dearer but you can still buy as much as you want. In a supply shock, a war, a sanction or a blocked shipping lane means the oil physically cannot reach you, or only by a longer, costlier route. Price becomes the symptom; availability is the disease.

India is unusually exposed here. It imports the large majority of the crude it uses, and a big share of that comes from the Gulf through one narrow stretch of water, the Strait of Hormuz. Much of its cooking gas and a large part of its liquefied natural gas come the same way. If that route is disrupted, refiners scramble for cargoes from further afield, freight and insurance costs jump, and the government faces an ugly choice: let pump prices rise and feed inflation, or cut fuel taxes and absorb the cost in its own budget.

So the energy pipe hits fast and lingers: prices react the same day, while the budget strain, the wider trade deficit and second-round inflation take months. It is the one channel that fills all four buckets at once. The oil chapter goes deeper.

sections.heading: India is no longer a slice of emerging Asia
sections.html:
Twenty years ago, global funds bought India as part of a basket called emerging Asia. If Thailand or Korea wobbled, India was sold too. Contagion by association.

Today India is large enough, liquid enough and different enough that global allocators increasingly treat it as a standalone market. That has two consequences, and they cut in opposite directions. Good news first: trouble in a neighbouring economy spreads to India less automatically than it used to. The bad news is subtler. India trades at a rich valuation premium to other emerging markets because investors expect its growth to last for decades. Much of its value lies in profits far in the future. And anything whose value lies far in the future is very sensitive to the global interest rate used to discount it. So India's premium now behaves like a long-dated bond: it swells when US rates fall and shrinks when they rise, even if Indian earnings do not change at all.

Then there is foreign policy. India's line is strategic autonomy: buy discounted oil from Russia, deepen ties with the US, compete with China, stay friendly with both Iran and the Gulf monarchies. It keeps options open, but India can be caught by sanctions or tariffs from several directions at once. In 2025 that stopped being theoretical, when Washington tied a tariff penalty directly to India's purchases of Russian crude.

sections.heading: Reading a foreign headline in five questions
sections.html:
Put it together and you have a short checklist for any piece of global news.

  1. Which pipe is it in? Rates, commodities, trade, flows or energy supply. Most big events use two or three.
  2. How fast does that pipe run? Days for money, a quarter for commodity costs, several quarters for trade, same-day for energy supply.
  3. Which bucket does it fill? The rupee, inflation, margins or equity flows.
  4. Who is on the other side? Every shock has winners. A weak rupee helps exporters. Dear metals help miners. A tariff on China can help an Indian rival.
  5. Is it a price shock or a quantity shock? Price shocks fade as prices adjust. Quantity shocks last until the route, the sanction or the war is resolved.

Run the opening headlines through it. The grumpy Fed is in the rates pipe: fast, worst for richly valued large caps. The tanker is in the energy pipe: immediate on fuel, slow on the budget. The tariff is in the trade pipe: slow, aimed at export clusters, visible in results quarters later. Same morning, three different trades.

history_title: how India got wired to the world

history.title: The plan that was shelved just in time
history.story:
In the spring of 1997 a committee chaired by S. S. Tarapore, a former deputy governor of the RBI, handed in a report with a bold idea: let money flow freely in and out of India and make the rupee fully convertible within a few years.

Weeks later, Thailand ran out of dollars to defend the baht and let it float. Within months the panic had spread to Indonesia, Malaysia and South Korea. Foreign money that had poured into those countries rushed out, currencies collapsed, banks failed and the IMF arrived with bailouts and harsh conditions. India, with its capital account still largely closed, saw its markets wobble but avoided the meltdown. The Tarapore roadmap quietly went into a drawer, and India opened up gradually instead.
history.lesson: A pipe that is closed cannot carry a panic; every time India opens a new channel to foreign money, it gains a source of funding and a route for contagion at the same time.

history.title: China joins the club
history.story:
At the end of 2001, after some fifteen years of negotiation and a big push from Premier Zhu Rongji, China joined the World Trade Organization. Within a few years it had become the workshop of the world.

For Indian manufacturers it changed the rules of the game. Makers of toys, bicycles, cheap electronics and later steel and solar panels found that the price of their product was no longer set in India or even in America. It was set by whatever a Chinese factory with spare capacity was willing to accept. Indian consumers got cheaper goods; Indian producers got a permanent, ruthless competitor.
history.lesson: For most manufactured goods India makes, the price-setter sits in China, so a slowdown there can flood India with cheap imports even when Indian demand is fine.

history.title: The text messages that hit a bank
history.story:
In September 2008 Lehman Brothers collapsed in New York, days after D. Subbarao had taken over as RBI governor. India's banks had little to do with American subprime mortgages, yet the shock arrived within weeks. Foreign investors pulled money out of Indian shares at a record pace that year, the Sensex lost more than half its value from its January peak, and overnight borrowing costs spiked as banks hoarded cash.

Then came the rumours. ICICI Bank, the country's largest private lender, had a small exposure to Lehman through its UK arm. Text messages started circulating claiming the bank was in trouble. Its shares plunged and panic spread among depositors. The RBI issued an unusual public statement that the bank was sound and had ample liquidity and the finance ministry joined in to reassure depositors. The panic passed, but a crisis thousands of miles away had reached an Indian bank counter through nothing more than fear.
history.lesson: Financial integration means global panics arrive in weeks, and they travel through flows and confidence long before they touch real business.

history.title: The trade war that opened a door
history.story:
In 2018 President Donald Trump slapped tariffs on steel and aluminium imports, India included, and then launched a far bigger tariff war against China. In 2019 Washington also ended the special duty-free access some Indian exports had enjoyed for decades. Delhi hit back with higher duties on American almonds, apples and walnuts.

But the bigger story was the one that unfolded slowly. Global companies began building second supply chains outside China. India's phone assembly industry, helped by government incentives, became one of the clearest beneficiaries, and in a few years iPhones were among India's fastest-growing exports.
history.lesson: Trade wars bring risk and opportunity at once; the China plus one shift is slow, but it is the kind of change that reshapes a country's export base.

history.title: The index that invited the world in
history.story:
In the autumn of 2023 JPMorgan announced that Indian government bonds would join its flagship emerging-market bond index, after years of India lobbying and foreign investors complaining about access. The inclusion began in June 2024, phased in over several months, and other index providers followed.

Index funds do not pick and choose; they buy what is in the index. So inclusion created a new, stickier stream of foreign money into Indian government debt. It also opened a new pipe. Bond funds that own India now sell it when they need to cut emerging-market risk, regardless of what is happening in India.
history.lesson: Every new door for foreign money is also a new exit; bond-index inclusion made India more stable on average and more connected in a panic.

history.title: The price of strategic autonomy
history.story:
In the summer of 2025 Washington imposed broad tariffs on Indian goods and then, in August, President Trump signed an order adding a further penalty tied directly to India's purchases of Russian crude. The combined tariff on many Indian exports doubled, putting India among the most heavily taxed of America's trading partners. Delhi called it unjustified and said it had acted in its national interest.

The hit was concentrated: textiles, gems and jewellery, seafood and auto parts faced the full duty, while electronics, iPhones and pharmaceuticals were spared. For investors, it was a lesson that keeping every option open can carry a bill in market access.
history.lesson: Geopolitics now reaches Indian earnings through the trade pipe; when India's strategic choices diverge from Washington's, export sectors pay first.

Energy supply: Brent is at [[val:brent]] a barrel, up [[val:brent_3m]] in three months, with the Hormuz route closed. Trade: talks with Washington have stalled. Capital flows: foreign investors have sold [[val:fii20]] over twenty sessions, while domestic institutions bought [[val:dii20]], which is why the rupee, at [[val:usdinr]] per dollar, is weak but not in free fall. Commodities: copper is still beating gold, so the world is not yet pricing a global recession.

That makes three of the five pipes adverse at once. India has handled each alone before; together they make the shock serious. The things to watch next are the Hormuz route reopening, any thaw in the trade talks, and whether domestic buying keeps absorbing foreign selling.
sowhat:
With rates, energy and trade all adverse, the map shows where pressure concentrates.

  • Most exposed are richly valued large caps that foreign funds own heavily.
  • Margin pressure builds a quarter or two out for heavy users of crude-based inputs: paints, tyres, chemicals, airlines and logistics.
  • Export clusters hit by US tariffs, such as textiles, gems and jewellery and seafood, face slow, grinding pressure on orders.
  • Relatively insulated are businesses that earn and spend mostly in India and do not depend on imported energy or foreign funding.
  • Natural hedges exist in metal producers and upstream energy, which earn more when global commodity prices rise, though policy can cap their windfall.

The picture flips when the pipes clear: a reopened Hormuz route, a trade deal with Washington, or US yields turning down. Two at once would change the regime.
